comments.author: Corbin
comments.text:
Guido van Rossum asked me directly about chardet’s dependencies and API stability when considering it for stdlib, but the effort died on the vine when the LGPL license (inherited from Mozilla’s original code) turned out to be a blocker. I’ve wanted to fix that ever since. … I later switched to 0BSD, a public-domain-equivalent license, which sidesteps the question of whether AI-generated code is copyrightable in the first place.


But Python stdlib code must be licensed with PSFL, so this was futile either way.

comments.author: intelfx
comments.text:
But Python stdlib code must be licensed with PSFL, so this was futile either way.


0BSD places no restrictions on use or redistribution of the work. It is obviously possible to sublicense such work, or any derivative of it, under the terms of PSFL (or any other terms, because any set of restrictions is a subset of "no restrictions"), so I'm not sure what exactly is futile?

comments.author: intelfx
comments.text:
A copyright license does not presume that one is the author. How did you arrive at this premise?


It's recently-settled law in the USA that chatbots can't be authors <...>


First, you appear to have answered an entirely different question from the one I asked.

I did not ask "can chatbots be authors". I asked why do you think that a copyright license presumes that the one offering it is the author.

This is obviously false: if I take a work licensed to me as "GPL-2.0-or-later" and then I distribute it to you under the terms of GPL-3.0-only, then I will have literally sublicensed a work that I'm not the author of. Alternatively, if I'm an evilcorp that made a free software product, received some contributions under a CLA, and then decided to switch the entire thing to BSL, then I, too, will have sublicensed some code that I did not author.

(Even so, the case you're citing is extremely narrow in scope and is entirely irrelevant here. And it was heard, btw, just not by the SCOTUS. See https://sfconservancy.org/blog/2026/mar/04/scotus-deny-cert-dc-circuit-thaler-appeal-llm-ai/ for details.)


So, when the GPL/LGPL say that "'The Program' refers to any copyrightable work licensed under this License," they directly indicate that non-copyrightable works aren't covered works.


Second, we were not talking about GPL/LGPL here (except for the example I gave above, which is illustrative). The canned text of (L)GPL may limit its applicability however it wishes; this has no bearing on our discussion.


Either way, even if something is not copyrightable (and I call into question your reasoning for why it must be the case), then it only means that the copyright law does not apply: one is not obligated to follow any license to use/derive/redistribute that work. I don't see where it means that the work cannot be used/derived from/redistributed, or that attaching a license to it is in itself illegal.

comments.author: mitsuhiko
comments.text:
It's recently-settled law in the USA that chatbots can't be authors


If that was the case (which it most likely will not be, but we really do not know), then chardet was just in the public domain rendering any discussion about copyrights and prior licenses on that work moot. Also the question about the standard library given that public domain code is already in the Python stdlib.

comments.author: lonjil
comments.text:
If that was the case (which it most likely will not be, but we really do not know), then chardet was just in the public domain rendering any discussion about copyrights and prior licenses on that work moot.


Something not being an author doesn't mean it can't have transformed a work in a non-creative (non-copyright granting) manner, in which case the original copyright would apply.

comments.author: mitsuhiko
comments.text: Can you elaborate? I'm not sure I understand what you mean here.

comments.author: intelfx
comments.text: Essentially, ~lonjil says that the phrase "not copyrightable" sometimes does double duty: something may be not independently copyrightable due to it being a pure mechanical transformation of the original work a.k.a. failing the originality threshold (in which case the copyright of the original work applies), but also something may be not copyrightable in principle because copyright law never applied in the first place (facts, ideas, or LLM outputs in which the human did not participate, subject to the present debate).

comments.author: mitsuhiko
comments.text:
But Python stdlib code must be licensed with PSFL, so this was futile either way.


That has historically not been correct and I'm pretty sure that is still not correct. The standard library even includes GPL code (readline). The issue here is that chardet was supposed to be used with the urllib library which would have caused many current users to be pulled into a *GPL dependency after a Python upgrade.
